groups.passage:
Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies leave Canada and the northern United States and fly as far as 3,000 miles to the mountains of central Mexico. No single butterfly makes the round trip. The monarchs that fly south in the fall are the great-grandchildren of the ones that left Mexico the spring before. Somehow, without ever having seen the forests where they will spend the winter, they find the same small groves of fir trees year after year.

Scientists have long wondered how such a fragile insect manages this journey. Experiments have shown that monarchs use the sun as a compass. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, the butterflies must also keep track of time, and researchers have found a kind of clock in the monarchs' antennae. On cloudy days, the butterflies may rely on Earth's magnetic field instead.

The migration is now in danger. Milkweed, the only plant on which monarchs lay their eggs, has disappeared from many farms and roadsides. Logging has thinned some of the winter forests in Mexico. In response, many schools and families have begun planting milkweed in their gardens, giving the travelers places to stop and raise the next generation.

groups.passage:
When Lena's family moved to a new town, she brought only one thing she truly cared about: a battered sketchbook. On her first day at the new school, she sat alone at lunch and drew the cafeteria windows, the trees beyond them, and a boy two tables away who was balancing a spoon on his nose.

The next day, the boy sat down across from her. "You drew me," he said, pointing at the page. Lena felt her face grow hot, but he only grinned. "You made my nose look heroic." By the end of the week, three more students were crowding around her table to see what she would draw next, and Lena realized she had stopped counting the days until summer.

groups.passage:
The first bicycles, built in the early 1800s, had no pedals at all. Riders sat on a wooden frame between two wheels and pushed themselves along with their feet, like a child on a scooter. These "walking machines" were fun for a short ride, but they were heavy and hard to steer.

In the 1860s, inventors attached pedals directly to the front wheel. Because one turn of the pedals meant one turn of the wheel, makers soon built front wheels as tall as five feet so that riders could go faster. These "high-wheelers" were fast but dangerous. A rider perched high above the front wheel could easily be thrown over the handlebars by a small rock.

The solution came in the 1880s with the "safety bicycle." It had two wheels of equal size and a chain that connected the pedals to the rear wheel. Gears let riders travel quickly without a giant wheel. The safety bicycle was so successful that almost every bicycle sold today still follows its basic design. Within a few years, cycling clubs had formed across Europe and America, and for the first time, ordinary people could travel miles from home on their own.

groups.passage: Most people think of deserts as places that are always hot, but the definition of a desert has nothing to do with temperature. A desert is any area that receives less than about ten inches of rain or snow in a year. By that measure, the largest desert on Earth is not the Sahara in Africa but Antarctica, the icy continent at the South Pole. Although Antarctica is covered with ice, very little new snow falls there each year. The ice has built up slowly over hundreds of thousands of years.
